sources.source: NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook, "EWMA Control Charts"

items.item: The EWMA is a statistic for monitoring a process that averages the data, giving less and less weight to data as it is further removed in time.

at.step: Reveal: three baseline families, three failure modes

items.item: A Shewhart chart's decision depends solely on the most recent measurement from the process.

at.step: Reveal: three baseline families, three failure modes

items.item: An EWMA's decision depends on an exponentially weighted average of all prior data, including the most recent measurement.

at.step: Reveal: three baseline families, three failure modes

items.item: The EWMA control procedure can be made sensitive to a small or gradual drift, whereas a Shewhart procedure can only react when the last point is outside a control limit.

at.step: Reveal: three baseline families, three failure modes

sources.source: NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook, "What are Control Charts?"

items.item: Control charts are used to routinely monitor quality.

at.step: Reveal: three baseline families, three failure modes

items.item: Control limits are chosen so that almost all data points fall within them as long as the process remains in control.

at.step: Reveal: three baseline families, three failure modes

items.item: A data point outside the control limits means the process is probably out of control.

at.step: Hook: a false alarm ignored, a real fault missed

items.item: Statistical methods to detect sequences or nonrandom patterns can be applied to the interpretation of control charts.

at.step: Reveal: three baseline families, three failure modes

items.item: A false alarm that fires on a normal ramp and a real fault that adapts into silence are opposite mistakes, not the same one.

at.step: Hook: a false alarm ignored, a real fault missed

items.item: Each baseline family is cheap to update per event, and each fails exactly where its own assumption breaks.

at.step: Reveal: three baseline families, three failure modes

items.item: A series with no history can't be trusted to alarm; a cold-start policy keeps it quiet until it earns one.

at.step: Reveal: sizing state at high cardinality

items.item: Grouping by shared cause turns a flood of per-series alerts into one alert an operator can actually act on.

at.step: Reveal: deduplication, grouping and suppression

items.item: A detector nobody trusts anymore is worse than no detector at all, since it still costs attention while returning nothing useful.

at.step: Reveal: alert precision as the detector's own metric

items.item: A backtest with a clean time-split shows a detector's own failure before go-live, not after a week of ignored alarms.

at.step: Reveal: backtesting on history, with a time-split

items.item: At ten times the series count, the next bottleneck is the per-series state's own memory footprint and churn-driven cold-start rate, not baseline accuracy.

at.step: Prove it: ten times the series

items.item: This topic leaves out statistical process control's own mechanics, OEE and downtime events, sensor-data quality, and the industrial data model as later-chapter forward pointers.
EWMA, seasonal decomposition, SPC rules, alert deduplication and grouping, and backtesting with a time-split are each established practice, not an emerging technique.
This closes the chapter's own method; the next chapter is the industrial domain these designs borrowed words from without teaching it.
